title: Chapter 10: Externalities, Public Goods, and Common Resources

questions.title: Defining an Economic Externality
questions.prompt_template: In microeconomics, what defines an externality in a market transaction?

hints.text: Focus on who bears the cost or receives the benefit and whether it is reflected in the market price.
An externality affects someone outside the buyer-seller exchange without compensation.

options_template.text: Any high production cost that forces a firm to raise its market price to buyers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Private Cost Confusion): Production costs paid by the firm and passed on through market prices are internalized private costs, not externalities.

options_template.text: An uncompensated cost or benefit imposed on a third party outside the market transaction.
options_template.feedback: Correct. An externality occurs whenever production or consumption spills an unpriced cost or benefit onto bystanders who are neither the buyer nor the seller.

options_template.text: A government excise tax collected from sellers to fund general public infrastructure.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Policy vs. Market Failure): A tax is a policy instrument, not the underlying market failure itself.

options_template.text: A voluntary discount offered by a seller to attract price-sensitive consumers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Priced Transaction Error): A discount occurs inside the voluntary buyer-seller exchange and involves no uncompensated third-party spillover.

questions.title: Marginal Social Cost and Overproduction
questions.prompt_template: When production generates a negative externality such as industrial air pollution, how does Marginal Social Cost ($MSC$) relate to Marginal Private Cost ($MPC$), and what is the unregulated market outcome?

hints.text: Compare the firm's private cost with the full cost borne by society, including bystanders.
Write $MSC$ as the sum of private and external marginal costs, then compare $MB = MPC$ with $MB = MSC$.

options_template.text: $MSC = MPC + MEC$, and the unregulated market overproduces ($Q_M > Q^*$).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Adding Marginal External Cost ($MEC$) to $MPC$ gives $MSC > MPC$. Because unregulated firms ignore $MEC$ and produce where $MB = MPC$, market output exceeds the socially efficient level $Q^*$.

options_template.text: $MSC = MPC - MEC$, and the unregulated market overproduces ($Q_M > Q^*$).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Reversal Error): External damages add to—rather than subtract from—the true social cost of production, so $MSC = MPC + MEC$.

options_template.text: $MSC = MPC + MEC$, and the unregulated market underproduces ($Q_M < Q^*$).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Quantity Direction Reversal): Because firms ignore external costs, their perceived marginal cost is artificially low, leading to overproduction ($Q_M > Q^*$), not underproduction.

options_template.text: $MSC = MPC$, because competitive market prices automatically incorporate third-party pollution damages.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Invisible Hand Overgeneralization): Competitive markets maximize social surplus only when all costs and benefits are priced; unpriced third-party harm drives a wedge between $MSC$ and $MPC$.

questions.title: Marginal Social Benefit and Underproduction
questions.prompt_template: Which statement accurately describes a market with a positive consumption externality, such as community vaccinations?

hints.text: Ask whether third parties gain unpriced benefits when an individual consumes the good.
Relate $MSB$, $MPB$, and $MEB$, then compare unregulated $MPB = MC$ against efficient $MSB = MC$.

options_template.text: $MSB = MPB - MEB$, causing the unregulated market to overproduce ($Q_M > Q^*$).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Reversal Error): External benefits add to private benefits ($MSB = MPB + MEB$), and ignoring them leads to underproduction rather than overproduction.

options_template.text: $MSB = MPB + MEB$, causing the unregulated market to overproduce ($Q_M > Q^*$).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Overproduction Confusion): Overproduction occurs with negative externalities. When buyers ignore external benefits ($MEB$), too few units are purchased ($Q_M < Q^*$).

options_template.text: $MSB = MPB + MEB$, causing the unregulated market to underproduce ($Q_M < Q^*$).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because private buyers consider only $MPB$ and ignore the spillover $MEB$ enjoyed by others, the free market stops at $MPB = MC$, leaving mutually beneficial units unproduced ($Q_M < Q^*$).

options_template.text: $MSB = MPB$, so competitive equilibrium already achieves $Q^*$ without any deadweight loss.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Externality Omission): A positive externality implies $MEB > 0$, creating a wedge between $MSB$ and $MPB$ and generating deadweight loss from foregone surplus.

questions.title: Why Socially Optimal Pollution Is Rarely Zero
questions.prompt_template: Why do economists conclude that the socially optimal level of industrial pollution is rarely zero?

hints.text: Recall the marginal rule for social efficiency: compare marginal benefit against marginal social cost.
Think about what happens to valuable economic output if society forces emissions all the way to $Q = 0$.

options_template.text: Because small amounts of pollution never impose any marginal external cost on bystanders.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Damage Assumption): Even low pollution levels can impose positive $MEC$; the key is comparing that marginal damage against the marginal benefit of the activity.

options_template.text: Because firms refuse to comply with environmental regulations unless emissions stay at $Q_M$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Compliance vs. Efficiency): Social optimality is defined by $MB = MSC$, not by firms' willingness to comply with regulation.

options_template.text: Because eliminating pollution always creates zero economic benefit for society.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Benefit Dismissal): Reducing pollution yields substantial health and environmental benefits whenever $MSC > MB$; efficiency simply stops once $MB = MSC$.

options_template.text: Because for initial units of vital production, marginal benefit exceeds marginal social cost ($MB > MSC$), so efficiency occurs where $MB = MSC$ at $Q^* > 0$.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Driving emissions to zero would eliminate essential production whose marginal benefit far exceeds the marginal harm of limited emissions; efficiency curbs only units where $MSC > MB$.

questions.title: Internalizing External Costs via a Pigouvian Tax
questions.prompt_template: How does an optimal Pigouvian tax correct a negative production externality in a competitive market?

hints.text: What does it mean to 'internalize' an externality?
Recall the exact formula linking the optimal corrective tax $t^*$ to Marginal External Cost.

options_template.text: It bans production outright so that $Q^*$ equals zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Pollution Fallacy): A Pigouvian tax does not prohibit production; it aligns private cost with social cost so output settles at $Q^*$ where $MB = MSC$.

options_template.text: It levies a per-unit tax equal to $MEC(Q^*)$ so firms face $MPC + t^* = MSC$ and voluntarily choose $Q^*$.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Setting $t^* = MEC(Q^*)$ internalizes the external damage into the firm's marginal decision, shifting private supply onto $MSC$ and restoring the socially efficient quantity $Q^*$.

options_template.text: It sets a price ceiling below $P_M$ so consumers pay less for polluting goods.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price Control Confusion): Lowering the price of a polluting good would stimulate even greater consumption and worsen overproduction.

options_template.text: It sets a per-unit tax equal to Marginal Private Cost ($MPC$) so firm profit falls to zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong Cost Base): The corrective tax must match the external harm $MEC(Q^*)$, not the firm's private production cost $MPC$.

questions.title: Correcting Positive Externalities with a Pigouvian Subsidy
questions.prompt_template: To restore social efficiency in a competitive market with a positive externality, at what level should regulators set a per-unit Pigouvian subsidy $s^*$?

hints.text: Think of the symmetric counterpart to a Pigouvian tax $t^* = MEC(Q^*)$.
What unpriced wedge separates $MSB$ from $MPB$ at the socially efficient quantity?

options_template.text: Equal to Marginal External Benefit evaluated at the socially efficient quantity: $s^* = MEB(Q^*)$.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Setting $s^* = MEB(Q^*)$ closes the exact gap between $MSB$ and $MPB$, expanding private consumption from $Q_M$ to $Q^*$.

options_template.text: Equal to Marginal Private Benefit evaluated at the unregulated quantity: $s^* = MPB(Q_M)$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Private vs. External Benefit Confusion): Buyers already internalize $MPB$; subsidizing $MPB$ would overshoot $Q^*$ unless $MPB$ happened to equal $MEB$.

options_template.text: Equal to the full Marginal Cost of production ($s^* = MC$) so the good is always free.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Full-Subsidy Fallacy): Making a good free ($P_b = 0$) is efficient only if $MPB(Q^*) = 0$; otherwise, subsidizing the full $MC$ causes overconsumption beyond $Q^*$.

options_template.text: Equal to Marginal Social Benefit ($s^* = MSB(Q^*)$) to double buyer willingness to pay.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Double-Counting Private Benefit): Since $MSB = MPB + MEB$, subsidizing all of $MSB$ double-counts the private benefit buyers already receive and induces overproduction.

questions.title: Foundational Conditions of the Coase Theorem
questions.prompt_template: According to the Coase Theorem, under what two conditions will private parties bargain directly to the socially efficient outcome $Q^*$ regardless of who initially holds the property right?

hints.text: Recall Ronald Coase's insight about private negotiation without government intervention.
Consider what parties must own legally and how costly it is to meet, negotiate, and enforce an agreement.

options_template.text: Equal incomes between both parties and a binding government price ceiling.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Irrelevant Assumptions): The Coase Theorem does not require equal wealth or price ceilings; price ceilings actually obstruct mutually beneficial bargaining.

options_template.text: Zero marginal external cost and a single monopoly producer.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (No-Externality Contradiction): If $MEC = 0$, there is no externality to bargain over in the first place.

options_template.text: Clearly defined property rights and low transaction costs.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When ownership is unambiguous and negotiation/enforcement costs are low, private bargaining captures all mutually beneficial trades and reaches $Q^*$ regardless of initial right assignment.

options_template.text: Strict command-and-control emissions quotas and public tax subsidies.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Government Intervention Confusion): The Coase Theorem explains when private bargaining achieves efficiency *without* government taxes or mandates.

questions.title: Cost Minimization Under Cap-and-Trade
questions.prompt_template: What mathematical condition characterizes the cost-minimizing allocation of pollution abatement across two firms under a cap-and-trade permit market?

hints.text: Think about when a firm prefers to abate one more ton itself versus buying a permit.
Compare each firm's marginal abatement cost ($MAC_i$) to the market permit price $p_{\text{permit}}$.

options_template.text: Both firms reduce emissions by the exact same number of tons ($a_1 = a_2$).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Uniform Mandate Fallacy): Equal tonnage cuts minimize cost only if firms have identical $MAC$ curves; when costs differ, uniform mandates waste resources.

options_template.text: The firm with the higher marginal abatement cost cuts all emissions while the lower-cost firm buys permits.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost-Direction Reversal): Efficiency requires the *lower*-cost abater to cut more pollution and sell spare permits to the *higher*-cost abater.

options_template.text: Total abatement costs are equal across firms ($C_1(a_1) = C_2(a_2)$).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Total vs. Marginal Confusion): Cost minimization equalizes *marginal* abatement costs across firms, not total abatement expenditures.

options_template.text: Each firm's marginal abatement cost equals the permit price ($MAC_1(a_1^*) = MAC_2(a_2^*) = p_{\text{permit}}$).
options_template.feedback: Correct. By the equimarginal principle, firms abate whenever $MAC_i < p_{\text{permit}}$ and buy permits whenever $MAC_i > p_{\text{permit}}$, equalizing marginal abatement costs at the lowest total cost.

questions.title: Distinguishing Excludability from Rivalry
questions.prompt_template: In economics, what is the difference between a good being 'excludable' and being 'rival in consumption'?

hints.text: One trait is about blocking non-payers; the other is about whether sharing depletes what remains.
Match 'excludable' to access/payment barriers and 'rival' to depletion of the physical unit.

options_template.text: Excludability means providers can prevent non-payers from using the good; rivalry means one person's consumption reduces the amount available for others.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Excludability concerns enforceable access control, whereas rivalry concerns whether simultaneous consumption diminishes availability for other users.

options_template.text: Excludability means one person's consumption depletes the good; rivalry means firms compete vigorously to sell the good.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Trait Swap & Colloquial Rivalry): This swaps the definition of rivalry onto excludability and confuses consumption rivalry with firm competition.

options_template.text: Excludability applies only to privately produced goods; rivalry applies only to government-provided services.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Provider-Identity Fallacy): Both traits describe physical characteristics of a good, regardless of whether the supplier is private or governmental.

options_template.text: Excludability means the good has zero marginal cost; rivalry means the good is too expensive for low-income households.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cost/Affordability Confusion): Affordability and zero marginal cost do not define excludability or rivalry.

questions.title: Identifying Club Goods
questions.prompt_template: A subscription streaming service and an uncongested toll bridge are both excludable yet non-rival in consumption. How do economists classify these goods?

hints.text: Recall the 2×2 matrix crossing Excludable/Non-Excludable with Rival/Non-Rival.
Which quadrant sits in the top-right: Excludable and Non-Rival?

options_template.text: Pure private goods
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Rivalry Omission): Private goods (such as coffee or laptops) are both excludable *and* rival in consumption.

options_template.text: Club goods
options_template.feedback: Correct. Club goods are excludable (providers can require subscriptions or tolls) and non-rival (one extra viewer or uncongested driver does not diminish the service for others).

options_template.text: Common resources
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Opposite Quadrant): Common resources are non-excludable and rival—the exact reverse of both traits.

options_template.text: Pure public goods
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Excludability Omission): Pure public goods are *non-excludable* as well as non-rival; because non-payers can be blocked here, these are club goods.

questions.title: The Free-Rider Problem in Public Goods
questions.prompt_template: Why do private markets systematically underprovide pure public goods such as coastal tsunami warning sirens or national defense?

hints.text: Ask what happens when a provider cannot bar non-payers from enjoying a good once it exists.
Connect non-excludability to the individual incentive to withhold payment.

options_template.text: Because public goods are rival in consumption, causing consumers to exhaust the stock immediately.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Common Resource Confusion): Rival depletion characterizes common resources (Tragedy of the Commons), whereas pure public goods are non-rival.

options_template.text: Because consumers place zero marginal benefit on pure public goods.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Valuation Fallacy): Consumers often place high value on sirens or defense; the failure is that they have an incentive to hide their willingness to pay and free ride.

options_template.text: Because non-excludability creates a free-rider problem in which rational individuals enjoy the benefit without paying, leaving private providers unable to cover costs.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Since non-payers cannot be excluded once the public good is supplied, individuals rationally free ride, causing private voluntary funding to fall far short of $Q^*$.

options_template.text: Because government regulations forbid private firms from building warning systems or conducting basic research.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Legal Prohibition Fallacy): The root cause of underprovision is economic—non-excludability and free riding—not a legal ban.

questions.topic: Common Resources & Tragedy of the Commons
questions.title: The Tragedy of the Commons
questions.prompt_template: Which combination of physical traits produces the Tragedy of the Commons—such as overfishing in open-ocean fisheries or severe congestion on free public highways?

hints.text: Think about whether anyone can enter the fishery or highway for free, and whether each user reduces what remains for others.
Match 'anyone can use it' to non-excludability and 'each user depletes it' to rivalry.

options_template.text: Excludable and rival in consumption
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Private Good Misclassification): Excludable and rival goods are private goods, where market prices prevent uncompensated depletion.

options_template.text: Excludable and non-rival in consumption
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Club Good Misclassification): Excludable and non-rival goods are club goods, which face natural-monopoly pricing issues rather than overexploitation.

options_template.text: Non-excludable and non-rival in consumption
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Public Good Misclassification): Non-excludable and non-rival goods are pure public goods, which suffer from *underprovision* (free riding), not overexploitation.

options_template.text: Non-excludable and rival in consumption
options_template.feedback: Correct. Common resources are non-excludable (open access at zero price) and rival (one user's catch or road space diminishes availability for others), driving overexploitation.

questions.topic: Economic Public Goods vs. Government Provision
questions.title: Economic Classification vs. Government Ownership
questions.prompt_template: Which of the following examples is a true economic public good (both non-excludable and non-rival), even though it may be supplied outside the government?

hints.text: Remember: 'public good' in economics depends on physical traits, not on who supplies the good.
Check each option for both non-excludability (cannot block non-payers) and non-rivalry (one user does not deplete it).

options_template.text: A state park that charges an admission fee at a gated entrance.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Government-Equals-Public-Good Fallacy): Because ticket gates exclude non-payers, a gated state park is excludable—not an economic public good—even though government operates it.

options_template.text: Privately written open-source software freely downloadable online, or free over-the-air radio broadcasts.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Anyone can access open-source software or unencrypted radio broadcasts (non-excludable), and one person's use does not diminish availability for others (non-rival).

options_template.text: A municipal city bus that requires a fare card to board and has limited seating.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Government-Equals-Public-Good Fallacy): Fare enforcement makes a city bus excludable, and limited seats make it rival when crowded.

options_template.text: An open-ocean salmon stock harvested by private commercial fleets.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Rivalry Omission): Open-ocean salmon are non-excludable but *rival*—one boat's catch reduces fish left for others—making them a common resource, not a public good.

questions.title: Vertical Gap Between MSC and MPC
questions.prompt_template: In a supply-and-demand diagram for a competitive market with a constant Marginal External Cost ($MEC = \$10$ per unit), how is the Marginal Social Cost ($MSC$) curve positioned relative to the Marginal Private Cost ($MPC$) curve?

hints.text: Recall $MSC(Q) = MPC(Q) + MEC$ with $MEC$ measured in dollars per unit on the vertical axis.
Adding a constant dollar amount at every quantity produces a parallel shift in which direction?

options_template.text: $MSC$ lies parallel and vertically above $MPC$ by exactly $\$10$ at every quantity.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because cost is plotted on the vertical axis and $MEC = \$10$ is constant, adding $\$10$ to $MPC(Q)$ shifts the curve vertically upward in parallel by $\$10$.

options_template.text: $MSC$ lies parallel and vertically below $MPC$ by exactly $\$10$ at every quantity.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift Direction Reversal): A downward shift would imply external costs *reduce* social cost; external damages increase social cost above private cost.

options_template.text: $MSC$ intersects $MPC$ at the vertical axis and diverges upward as quantity increases.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Constant vs. Increasing MEC Confusion): A shared intercept with a steeper slope occurs when $MEC(Q)$ rises linearly from zero with output, not when $MEC$ is constant at $\$10$.

options_template.text: $MSC$ shifts horizontally to the right of $MPC$ by $10$ units at every price.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Axis Confusion): $MEC = \$10$/unit is a vertical cost wedge (dollars/unit), and higher marginal costs shift supply *leftward*/upward, never rightward.

questions.title: Comparing Unregulated and Efficient Price and Quantity
questions.prompt_template: In a negative production externality diagram with downward-sloping $MB$ and upward-sloping $MPC$ and $MSC$, how does the unregulated market equilibrium $(Q_M, P_M)$ compare to the socially efficient equilibrium $(Q^*, P^*)$?

hints.text: Locate $E_M$ where $MB = MPC$ and $E^*$ where $MB = MSC$.
Since $MSC$ lies above $MPC$, trace leftward and upward along the downward-sloping $MB$ curve from $E_M$ to $E^*$.

options_template.text: $Q_M > Q^*$ and $P_M > P^*$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Price Direction Error): Moving up along a downward-sloping demand ($MB$) curve to the smaller quantity $Q^*$ raises price, so $P^*$ is higher than $P_M$ ($P_M < P^*$).

options_template.text: $Q_M < Q^*$ and $P_M > P^*$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Positive Externality Swap): Underproduction ($Q_M < Q^*$) characterizes a positive externality, not a negative production externality.

options_template.text: $Q_M > Q^*$ and $P_M < P^*$.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because firms ignore external costs, the unregulated market overproduces ($Q_M > Q^*$) at an artificially low market price ($P_M < P^*$).

options_template.text: $Q_M < Q^*$ and $P_M < P^*$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Demand Shift Confusion): A negative production externality moves equilibrium along $MB$ between $MPC$ and $MSC$, so price and quantity move in opposite directions.

questions.title: Locating the Negative Externality Deadweight Loss Triangle
questions.prompt_template: On a standard negative production externality graph ($MB$, $MPC$, and $MSC$), which geometric region represents the Deadweight Loss ($DWL$) caused by unregulated production at $Q_M$?

hints.text: Identify which specific units destroy net social welfare: units where $MSC$ exceeds $MB$.
Look at the interval between $Q^*$ and $Q_M$ and identify the vertical boundary at $Q_M$.

options_template.text: The triangle between $Q = 0$ and $Q^*$, bounded above by $MB$ and below by $MSC$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Social Surplus vs. DWL Confusion): The area between $MB$ and $MSC$ from $0$ to $Q^*$ is the *positive* net social surplus generated by efficient production, not deadweight loss.

options_template.text: The triangle between $Q^*$ and $Q_M$, bounded above by $MSC$ and below by $MB$, pointing leftward to $E^*$.
options_template.feedback: Correct. On every overproduced unit from $Q^*$ to $Q_M$, true social cost $MSC$ exceeds social benefit $MB$; integrating $(MSC - MB)$ yields this triangle pointing toward $E^*$.

options_template.text: The parallelogram between $MPC$ and $MSC$ extending from $Q = 0$ all the way to $Q_M$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Total External Cost vs. DWL Confusion): The full strip between $MPC$ and $MSC$ equals *total external cost*, most of which is outweighed by $MB > MSC$ on units $0$ to $Q^*$.

options_template.text: The triangle between $Q^*$ and $Q_M$, bounded above by $MB$ and below by $MPC$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong Boundary Curves): Between $Q^*$ and $Q_M$, $MB$ lies above $MPC$ (which is why private firms produce those units), but the welfare loss equals the gap between $MSC$ and $MB$.

questions.title: Graphing an Increasing Marginal External Cost
questions.prompt_template: Suppose environmental damage accelerates as factory output expands, so Marginal External Cost rises proportionally with quantity ($MEC(Q) = cQ$ with $c > 0$). How does the $MSC$ curve compare graphically to the linear $MPC$ curve?

hints.text: Evaluate $MSC(Q) = MPC(Q) + cQ$ at $Q = 0$ and check its slope relative to $MPC(Q)$.
At $Q = 0$, $MEC(0) = 0$; as $Q$ rises, what happens to the vertical distance $MSC(Q) - MPC(Q)$?

options_template.text: $MSC$ is parallel to $MPC$ and shifted vertically upward by $c$ dollars.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Constant-Shift Assumption): A parallel shift happens only when $MEC$ is constant; here $MEC = cQ$ grows with $Q$, changing the slope.

options_template.text: $MSC$ starts higher than $MPC$ at $Q = 0$ and flattens out to merge with $MPC$ at high quantities.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Direction Reversal): Because $MEC(Q) = cQ$ starts at $0$ and increases with $Q$, the two curves start together and *diverge*, rather than converging.

options_template.text: $MSC$ is identical to $MPC$ because marginal external cost is zero at $Q = 0$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Intercept-Only Fallacy): Sharing a vertical intercept at $Q = 0$ does not make two curves identical when their slopes differ for all $Q > 0$.

options_template.text: $MSC$ shares the same vertical intercept as $MPC$ at $Q = 0$ but has a steeper upward slope, widening the vertical gap as $Q$ increases.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Since $MEC(0) = 0$ and $MEC(Q) = cQ$ increases with $Q$, $MSC$ starts at the same intercept as $MPC$ and rotates upward with a steeper slope.

questions.title: Reading a Positive Consumption Externality Diagram
questions.prompt_template: In a diagram of a positive consumption externality (with constant $MEB > 0$ and horizontal $MC$), where do the $MSB$ curve and the Deadweight Loss triangle appear relative to $MPB$ and $Q_M$?

hints.text: Add $MEB > 0$ vertically to $MPB$ to locate $MSB$.
Identify which unproduced units between $Q_M$ and $Q^*$ have $MSB > MC$.

options_template.text: $MSB$ lies vertically above $MPB$ by $MEB$, and the DWL triangle lies between $Q_M$ and $Q^*$ bounded above by $MSB$ and below by $MC$, pointing rightward to $E^*$.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Because $MSB = MPB + MEB$, the social benefit curve shifts vertically upward; on missing units from $Q_M$ to $Q^*$, $MSB > MC$, forming a DWL triangle pointing right toward $E^*$.

options_template.text: $MSB$ lies vertically below $MPB$ by $MEB$, and the DWL triangle lies to the left of $Q_M$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Shift Direction Reversal): External benefits raise social benefit above private benefit ($MSB > MPB$), shifting the curve upward and placing $Q^*$ to the right of $Q_M$.

options_template.text: $MSB$ lies vertically above $MPB$, and the DWL triangle lies to the right of $Q^*$ where $MC > MSB$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Overproduction Region Error): Units beyond $Q^*$ are not produced in an unregulated positive-externality market; the welfare loss comes from *missing* units between $Q_M$ and $Q^*$.

options_template.text: $MSB$ coincides with $MPB$, while the $MC$ curve shifts downward by $MEB$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Benefit vs. Cost Curve Mix-Up): A consumption spillover alters *Marginal Social Benefit*, not the physical production cost curve $MC$.

questions.title: Effect of an Optimal Pigouvian Tax on Supply and Equilibrium
questions.prompt_template: Starting from an unregulated negative-externality equilibrium $E_M(Q_M, P_M)$, what happens graphically when the government levies an optimal Pigouvian tax $t^* = MEC(Q^*)$ on producers?

hints.text: Track how a per-unit tax on producers shifts the private supply curve $MPC$.
Observe where the post-tax private supply curve intersects $MB$ and what happens to the DWL triangle.

options_template.text: The $MB$ curve shifts downward by $t^*$, reducing both price and quantity.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong Curve Shift): A statutory tax on producers shifts their marginal cost curve upward rather than shifting buyers' underlying marginal benefit curve.

options_template.text: Private marginal cost shifts upward from $MPC$ onto $MSC = MPC + t^*$, moving equilibrium up along $MB$ from $E_M$ to $E^*$ and eliminating DWL.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Adding $t^* = MEC(Q^*)$ to $MPC$ aligns private supply with $MSC$, moving the market along $MB$ to $E^*(Q^*, P^*)$ and driving deadweight loss to zero.

options_template.text: Both $MPC$ and $MSC$ shift upward by $t^*$, leaving the vertical wedge between them unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Double-Shifting Social Cost): A tax is a transfer from firms to the government, not a new physical resource cost, so $MSC$ does not shift—only private cost $MPC + t^*$ shifts up to meet $MSC$.

options_template.text: Private marginal cost shifts downward by $t^*$, increasing quantity beyond $Q_M$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Tax vs. Subsidy Confusion): A tax raises private marginal cost (upward shift), whereas a subsidy lowers it.

questions.title: Reading Buyer Price, Seller Net Price, and Tax Revenue
questions.prompt_template: In a diagram showing an optimal Pigouvian tax $t^* = MEC$ levied on producers at the efficient quantity $Q^*$, how are the buyer price $P^*$, seller net price $P_s$, and total tax revenue represented?

hints.text: At $Q^*$, check the height of $MSC = MPC + t^*$ (on $MB$) versus the height of pre-tax $MPC$.
Tax revenue equals per-unit tax multiplied by taxed quantity: what rectangle has height $t^*$ and width $Q^*$?

options_template.text: Buyers pay $P_M$, sellers receive $P^*$, and tax revenue is the triangle between $Q^*$ and $Q_M$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Triangle vs. Rectangle Confusion): Tax revenue is a rectangle ($t^* \times Q^*$), not the DWL triangle, and buyers pay the higher post-tax price $P^*$.

options_template.text: Buyers and sellers both face $P^*$, and tax revenue equals $P^* \times Q^*$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Total Expenditure vs. Tax Revenue): $P^* \times Q^*$ is total buyer spending; sellers remit $t^*$ per unit to the government and keep only $P_s = P^* - t^*$.

options_template.text: Buyers pay $P^*$, sellers receive $P_s = P^* - t^*$, and tax revenue is the rectangle of height $t^*$ and width $Q_M$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Pre-Tax Quantity Error): Tax revenue is collected only on the units actually sold *after* the tax ($Q^*$), not the larger pre-tax quantity $Q_M$.

options_template.text: Buyers pay $P^*$ (on $MB$ at $Q^*$), sellers net $P_s = P^* - t^*$ (on pre-tax $MPC$ at $Q^*$), and tax revenue is the rectangle of width $Q^*$ and height $(P^* - P_s) = t^*$.
options_template.feedback: Correct. At $Q^*$, the tax creates a vertical wedge of height $t^*$ between buyer price $P^*$ and seller net price $P_s$, generating rectangular revenue $R = t^* \times Q^*$.

questions.title: Graphical Effect of a Pigouvian Subsidy with Constant Marginal Cost
questions.prompt_template: Consider a positive externality market with downward-sloping $MPB$, parallel $MSB = MPB + MEB$, and horizontal supply at constant $MC$. When the government provides an optimal Pigouvian subsidy $s^* = MEB$ per unit, what happens on the graph?

hints.text: Check what price sellers must receive (constant $MC$) and what out-of-pocket price buyers pay ($P_b = MC - s^*$).
Verify where $MPB(Q)$ equals $P_b = MC - s^*$ relative to $MSB(Q) = MC$.

options_template.text: The out-of-pocket buyer price rises to $MC + s^*$, shrinking quantity below $Q_M$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Subsidy Sign Error): A subsidy lowers—rather than raises—the buyer's effective price, expanding consumption from $Q_M$ to $Q^*$.

options_template.text: Both $MPB$ and $MSB$ shift upward by $s^*$, pushing quantity past $Q^*$ into overconsumption.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Double-Shifting Social Benefit): The subsidy transfers funds to internalize $MEB$ without altering true social benefit $MSB$; private demand rises onto $MSB$, stopping cleanly at $Q^*$.

options_template.text: The buyer's effective out-of-pocket price drops to $P_b = MC - s^*$ (equivalently shifting private demand up to $MSB$), moving output from $Q_M$ to $Q^*$ and eliminating the underproduction DWL triangle.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Lowering the buyer's net price by $s^* = MEB$ induces buyers to move down $MPB$ to $Q^*$ (where $MPB(Q^*) = MC - s^* \iff MSB(Q^*) = MC$), capturing the entire DWL triangle.

options_template.text: Quantity remains stuck at $Q_M$ because horizontal $MC$ prevents suppliers from expanding output.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply Elasticity Misinterpretation): A horizontal $MC$ curve is *perfectly elastic*, meaning suppliers gladly expand output from $Q_M$ to $Q^*$ at constant unit cost $MC$.

questions.topic: Over-Taxing Beyond the Optimal Pigouvian Rate
questions.title: Welfare Consequence of Setting a Corrective Tax Too High
questions.prompt_template: Suppose regulators overestimate environmental damages and levy a per-unit tax $t > MEC$ on a polluting industry. What does the supply-and-demand graph show at the resulting post-tax quantity $Q_{\text{tax}}$?

hints.text: Compare the shifted post-tax supply curve $MPC + t$ with the true $MSC = MPC + MEC$.
Ask whether $Q_{\text{tax}}$ is greater than or less than $Q^*$, and compare $MB$ to $MSC$ on the lost units.

options_template.text: $MPC + t$ lies above $MSC$, reducing output below $Q^*$ ($Q_{\text{tax}} < Q^*$) and creating a new DWL triangle from underproduction on units where $MB > MSC$.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Over-taxing pushes private marginal cost above true social cost, choking off socially beneficial units between $Q_{\text{tax}}$ and $Q^*$ where $MB > MSC$.

options_template.text: $MPC + t$ lies above $MSC$, reducing output below $Q^*$ and further increasing total social surplus because less pollution is always better.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Pollution Fallacy): Once output falls below $Q^*$, each foregone unit sacrifices more marginal benefit ($MB$) than the marginal social cost ($MSC$) saved, lowering net welfare.

options_template.text: $MPC + t$ lies below $MSC$, leaving residual overproduction between $Q^*$ and $Q_{\text{tax}}$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inequality Reversal): Residual overproduction occurs when a tax is set *too low* ($t < MEC$), not too high ($t > MEC$).

options_template.text: Equilibrium remains fixed at $Q^*$ because markets cannot produce less than the socially efficient output.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Market-Floor Fallacy): Markets respond to private incentives ($MB = MPC + t$); excessive taxation easily drives output below $Q^*$.

questions.title: Aggregating Demand for Public Goods vs. Private Goods
questions.prompt_template: Graphically, why do economists sum individual marginal benefit curves vertically to obtain Marginal Social Benefit ($MSB$) for a pure public good, rather than summing horizontally as they do for a private good?

hints.text: Ask which variable—price or quantity—is shared identically by every consumer of a non-rival good.
For a fixed quantity $Q$ of a public good, how do we find society's combined willingness to pay?

options_template.text: Because every citizen pays the exact same market price and consumes a separate, mutually exclusive quantity of the public good.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Private-Good Rule Swap): Paying the same price while consuming separate quantities describes *private goods*, which require horizontal summation ($Q = Q_1 + Q_2$).

options_template.text: Because non-rivalry means every citizen consumes the exact same quantity $Q$ simultaneously, so society's total willingness to pay at each $Q$ equals the vertical sum of individual marginal benefits ($MB_1 + MB_2$).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Since one siren or defense shield protects everyone at once, holding $Q$ fixed and summing vertical heights ($MB_i$) captures the joint social value of that marginal unit.

options_template.text: Because vertical summation ensures that the $MSB$ curve is always flatter than every individual $MB_i$ curve.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope Direction Error): Summing downward-sloping curves vertically *steepens* the combined curve (adding slopes) rather than flattening it.

options_template.text: Because public goods are excludable, allowing firms to charge higher prices through vertical price discrimination.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Excludability Misclassification): Pure public goods are non-excludable, and vertical summation reflects non-rival simultaneous consumption rather than price discrimination.

questions.topic: Kinked MSB Curve for Public Goods
questions.title: Explaining the Kink in a Two-Town Public-Good MSB Curve
questions.prompt_template: In a two-town public-good graph where Town 1 has $MB_1 = 50 - Q$ and Town 2 has $MB_2 = 30 - Q$ (with $MB_i \ge 0$), why does the vertically summed $MSB$ curve exhibit a sharp kink at $Q = 30$?

hints.text: Evaluate $MB_2 = 30 - Q$ at $Q = 30$ and check what happens for $Q > 30$.
Can Town 2's marginal willingness to pay become negative, or does it stop at $\$0$?

options_template.text: Because marginal cost $MC$ suddenly jumps upward at $Q = 30$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Supply vs. Demand Confusion): The kink is a property of the *demand-side* $MSB$ schedule, completely independent of the $MC$ curve.

options_template.text: Because Town 1 stops valuing additional units at $Q = 30$, leaving only Town 2 in the market.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Town-Identity Swap): Town 1's $MB_1 = 50 - Q$ is still $\$20$ at $Q = 30$; it is *Town 2*'s marginal benefit ($30 - Q$) that reaches $\$0$ at $Q = 30$.

options_template.text: Because for $Q > 30$, Town 2's negative willingness to pay subtracts from Town 1's benefit and makes $MSB$ steeper.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Negative-WTP Fallacy): Non-negative marginal willingness to pay means Town 2 contributes $\$0$—not a negative value—beyond $Q = 30$, so $MSB$ becomes *flatter*, not steeper.

options_template.text: Because Town 2's marginal benefit reaches $\$0$ at $Q = 30$ and cannot turn negative, so for $Q > 30$ the $MSB$ curve merges with $MB_1$ and becomes flatter.
options_template.feedback: Correct. For $0 \le Q \le 30$, both towns contribute ($MSB = 80 - 2Q$, slope $-2$); beyond $Q = 30$, $MB_2 = 0$, so $MSB = MB_1 = 50 - Q$ (slope $-1$), creating the kink at $(30, \$20)$.

questions.topic: Public Good Unilateral vs. Efficient Provision Graph
questions.title: Identifying Surplus Gains on a Public-Good Vertical Summation Graph
questions.prompt_template: On a two-town public-good graph with constant $MC$, Town 1 acts alone to provide $Q_1$ where $MB_1(Q_1) = MC$, while Town 2 free rides ($Q_2 = 0$). Which area on the graph measures the net social surplus gained by coordinating to move from $Q_1$ to $Q^*$ (where $MSB = MC$)?

hints.text: Compare the height of $MSB$ against $MC$ on every added unit between $Q_1$ and $Q^*$.
Look for the triangle bounded above by $MSB$ and below by $MC$ over the interval $[Q_1, Q^*]$.

options_template.text: The rectangle of height $MC$ and width $(Q^* - Q_1)$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Total Cost vs. Net Surplus): $MC \times (Q^* - Q_1)$ is the total resource *cost* of installing the extra units, ignoring the larger marginal social benefit $MSB$.

options_template.text: The triangle below $MB_1$ and above $MC$ from $Q = 0$ to $Q_1$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Already-Captured Surplus): That region measures Town 1's unilateral private surplus already captured at $Q_1$, not the *additional* gain from moving to $Q^*$.

options_template.text: The triangle between $Q_1$ and $Q^*$, bounded above by $MSB$ and below by $MC$.
options_template.feedback: Correct. On each unit from $Q_1$ to $Q^*$, joint marginal social benefit $MSB$ exceeds $MC$, so the triangular area $\frac{1}{2}(Q^* - Q_1)(MSB(Q_1) - MC)$ equals the recovered net social surplus.

options_template.text: The triangle between $Q_1$ and $Q^*$, bounded above by $MC$ and below by $MB_1$.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignoring Town 2's Benefit): Measuring below $MC$ down to $MB_1$ captures only Town 1's private shortfall and omits Town 2's positive spillover benefit $MB_2$.

questions.title: Moving Across Quadrants When Congestion Strikes a Free Highway
questions.prompt_template: On the four-quadrant goods classification matrix (Excludability vs. Rivalry), how does a free public highway shift when traffic increases from an empty midnight roadway to bumper-to-bumper rush hour?

hints.text: Ask whether the highway's excludability changes (still free, no tolls) and whether rivalry changes when traffic jams form.
Trace the move from (Non-Excludable, Non-Rival) to (Non-Excludable, Rival).

options_template.text: It shifts horizontally from a Public Good (non-excludable, non-rival) to a Common Resource (non-excludable, rival).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Without tolls, the road stays non-excludable, but rush-hour congestion makes road space rival—each added car slows everyone else—shifting it into the Common Resource quadrant.

options_template.text: It shifts vertically from a Public Good to a Club Good (excludable, non-rival).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Tolling vs. Congestion Confusion): Becoming a club good requires adding an exclusion mechanism (like tolls) while remaining uncongested; congestion changes *rivalry*, not excludability.

options_template.text: It shifts diagonally from a Public Good to a Private Good (excludable, rival).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Missing Exclusion Mechanism): Without tolls or gates, rush-hour drivers still cannot be excluded from entering the free highway, so it is a common resource rather than a private good.

options_template.text: It remains permanently in the Public Good quadrant because highways are built by the government.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Government-Identity Fallacy): Classification depends on physical rivalry and excludability—not government ownership—and severe congestion makes road capacity rival.

questions.title: Computing Socially Efficient Quantity and Price
questions.prompt_template: A competitive chemical market has linear marginal benefit $MB = 120 - 2Q$, marginal private cost $MPC = 20 + 2Q$, and a constant marginal external cost $MEC = \$16$ per unit (assuming no consumption externalities). What are the socially efficient quantity $Q^*$ and price $P^*$?

hints.text: First construct Marginal Social Cost using $MSC = MPC + MEC$.
Set $MB = MSC$ to solve for $Q^*$, then substitute $Q^*$ into $MB$ (or $MSC$) to find $P^*$.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Ignored External Cost): Setting $MB = MPC$ ($120 - 2Q = 20 + 2Q$) yields the *unregulated* market equilibrium $(Q_M = 25, P_M = \$70)$, not the socially efficient outcome.
Diagnostic fallacy (Sign Reversal Error): Subtracting $MEC$ ($MPC - 16 = 4 + 2Q$) instead of adding it yields $4Q = 116 \implies Q = 29$; external harm increases social cost.

Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong Curve Substitution): $Q^* = 21$ is right, but substituting $21$ into $MPC$ ($20 + 42 = \$62$) gives the pre-tax seller net price rather than the efficient market price $P^* = MB(21) = \$78$.

questions.title: Calculating Deadweight Loss from Overproduction
questions.prompt_template: In a competitive market with linear curves $MB = 90 - Q$, $MPC = 10 + Q$, and constant $MEC = \$12$ per unit (with no consumption externalities), what is the Deadweight Loss ($DWL$) caused by unregulated production?

hints.text: Compute both the unregulated quantity $Q_M$ (where $MB = MPC$) and the socially efficient quantity $Q^*$ (where $MB = MSC = MPC + 12$).
Apply the triangle area formula $DWL = \frac{1}{2} \times (Q_M - Q^*) \times MEC$.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Triangle Factor): Multiplying $(Q_M - Q^*) \times MEC = 6 \times \$12 = \$72$ calculates a rectangle instead of a triangle; remember the $\frac{1}{2}$ factor.
Diagnostic fallacy (Double-Halving Error): Dividing $\$72$ by $4$ instead of $2$ understates the area of the DWL triangle $\frac{1}{2} \times 6 \times \$12 = \$36$.
Correct. $Q_M = 40$ (from $90 - Q = 10 + Q$) and $Q^* = 34$ (from $90 - Q = 22 + Q$), so $DWL = \frac{1}{2} \times (40 - 34) \times \$12 = \frac{1}{2} \times 6 \times \$12 = \$36$.

Diagnostic fallacy (Total External Cost Confusion): Multiplying $Q_M \times MEC = 40 \times \$12 = \$480$ computes total external damages across all units rather than deadweight loss on the $6$ overproduced units.

questions.topic: Pigouvian Tax Revenue & Net Seller Price
questions.title: Computing Seller Net Price and Pigouvian Tax Revenue
questions.prompt_template: A competitive market has $MB = 110 - Q$, $MPC = 30 + Q$, and a constant marginal external cost $MEC = \$20$ per unit. If the government imposes the optimal Pigouvian tax $t^* = \$20$ per unit on producers, what are the seller's net-of-tax price $P_s$ and total government tax revenue $R$?

hints.text: Find the efficient post-tax equilibrium $(Q^*, P^*)$ where $MB = MSC = MPC + 20$.
Then compute $P_s = P^* - t^*$ and $R = t^* \times Q^*$.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Pre-Tax Equilibrium Error): Using unregulated $Q_M = 40$ and $P_M = \$70$ ignores the output reduction caused by the tax; revenue must be computed at $Q^* = 30$.
Correct. $MSC = 50 + Q$, so $110 - Q^* = 50 + Q^* \implies Q^* = 30$ and $P^* = \$80$. Sellers keep $P_s = \$80 - \$20 = \$60$, and tax revenue is $R = \$20 \times 30 = \$600$.
Diagnostic fallacy (Buyer vs. Seller Price Confusion): $\$80$ is the gross price paid by *buyers* ($P^*$); after remitting the $\$20$ tax, sellers net only $P_s = \$80 - \$20 = \$60$.

Diagnostic fallacy (Subtracted Tax from Pre-Tax Price): Subtracting $\$20$ from the unregulated price $P_M = \$70$ yields $\$50$, forgetting that the market price rises from $\$70$ to $P^* = \$80$ so buyers and sellers share the tax burden.

questions.topic: Optimal Pigouvian Tax with Increasing MEC
questions.title: Evaluating $t^* = MEC(Q^*)$ When External Cost Rises with Output
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a competitive industry faces $MB = 100 - Q$, $MPC = 10 + Q$, and an increasing marginal external cost $MEC(Q) = 0.5Q$. What per-unit Pigouvian tax $t^*$ achieves the socially efficient output $Q^*$?

hints.text: First form $MSC(Q) = MPC(Q) + MEC(Q)$ and solve $MB(Q^*) = MSC(Q^*)$ for $Q^*$.
Remember the Pigouvian rule: evaluate $MEC(Q)$ at the socially efficient quantity $Q^*$, not at $Q_M$.

options_template.text: $\$22.50$ per unit
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Evaluated MEC at Unregulated Quantity): $Q_M = 45$ gives $MEC(45) = \$22.50$, which over-taxes the industry; $t^*$ must be evaluated at $Q^* = 36$.

options_template.text: $\$36.00$ per unit
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Quantity-Tax Swap): $36$ is the socially efficient *quantity* $Q^*$; you still need to plug $Q^* = 36$ into $MEC(Q) = 0.5Q$.

options_template.text: $\$9.00$ per unit
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope Halving Error): Multiplying $Q^* = 36$ by $0.25$ instead of $0.5$ gives half the required corrective tax.

options_template.text: $\$18.00$ per unit

questions.title: Computing Efficient Quantity, Subsidy Rate, and Buyer Price
questions.prompt_template: Suppose residential solar installations have linear marginal private benefit $MPB = 90 - 3Q$, marginal social benefit $MSB = 120 - 3Q$, and constant marginal cost $MC = \$45$ (with $Q$ in thousands of units and no external production costs). What are the socially efficient quantity $Q^*$, optimal Pigouvian subsidy $s^*$, and buyer out-of-pocket price $P_b$?

hints.text: Set $MSB = MC$ to find $Q^*$, and compute $s^* = MEB = MSB - MPB$.
Subtract the subsidy $s^*$ from the seller's constant cost $MC$ to find the buyer's net price $P_b$.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Unregulated Quantity Error): Solving $MPB = MC$ ($90 - 3Q = 45$) yields the unregulated quantity $Q_M = 15$ thousand rather than $Q^* = 25$ thousand.

Correct. Setting $120 - 3Q^* = 45$ gives $3Q^* = 75 \implies Q^* = 25$ thousand. The optimal subsidy is $s^* = MSB - MPB = \$30$, lowering the buyer's out-of-pocket price to $P_b = \$45 - \$30 = \$15$ (matching $MPB(25) = 90 - 75 = \$15$).
Diagnostic fallacy (Added Subsidy to Price): A subsidy *reduces* the buyer's out-of-pocket price ($\$45 - \$30 = \$15$); adding $\$30$ to $\$45$ treats the subsidy like a tax.
Diagnostic fallacy (Swapped Subsidy and Buyer Price): The external benefit wedge is $MSB - MPB = 120 - 90 = \$30$ (so $s^* = \$30$), leaving buyers to pay $P_b = \$15$, not vice versa.

questions.topic: Positive Externality DWL Avoided & Subsidy Outlay
questions.title: Quantifying Avoided Deadweight Loss and Total Subsidy Expenditure
questions.prompt_template: Community immunization doses have $MPB = 70 - Q$, a constant marginal external benefit $MEB = \$14$ per dose, and a constant marginal cost $MC = \$40$ per dose (where $Q$ is in thousands of doses). Under an optimal Pigouvian subsidy $s^* = \$14$, what are the Deadweight Loss avoided and total public subsidy outlay?

hints.text: First solve $MPB = MC$ for $Q_M$ and $MSB = MPB + 14 = MC$ for $Q^*$.
Compute $DWL_{\text{avoided}} = \frac{1}{2}(Q^* - Q_M) \times MEB$, and remember the subsidy is paid on *all* $Q^*$ doses.

options_template.text: DWL avoided $= \$196$ thousand; subsidy outlay $= \$616$ thousand
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Triangle Factor): Multiplying $(44 - 30) \times \$14 = \$196$ thousand omits the $\frac{1}{2}$ factor in the DWL triangle.

options_template.text: DWL avoided $= \$98$ thousand; subsidy outlay $= \$420$ thousand
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Pre-Subsidy Quantity Error): Multiplying $\$14 \times 30$ thousand ($Q_M$) understates budget expenditure because the subsidy must be paid on the expanded quantity $Q^* = 44$ thousand.

options_template.text: DWL avoided $= \$98$ thousand; subsidy outlay $= \$616$ thousand
options_template.feedback: Correct. $Q_M = 30$ thousand and $Q^* = 44$ thousand (from $84 - Q^* = 40$). Thus $DWL_{\text{avoided}} = \frac{1}{2}(44 - 30)(\$14) = \$98$ thousand, and total outlay $= \$14 \times 44\text{ thousand} = \$616$ thousand.

options_template.text: DWL avoided $= \$98$ thousand; subsidy outlay $= \$196$ thousand
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Marginal-Units-Only Outlay Error): Multiplying $\$14 \times 14$ thousand pays the subsidy only on the newly added doses; a per-unit market subsidy applies to all $44$ thousand doses purchased.

questions.title: Solving for Cost-Minimizing Abatement and Permit Price
questions.prompt_template: Two regulated factories must jointly reduce emissions by $45$ tons under a cap-and-trade program. Factory A's marginal abatement cost is $MAC_A = 2a_A$, and Factory B's is $MAC_B = 4a_B$ (in dollars per ton). What abatement quantities $(a_A^*, a_B^*)$ and market permit price $p_{\text{permit}}$ minimize total abatement cost?

hints.text: Apply the equimarginal condition $MAC_A = MAC_B$ to express $a_A$ in terms of $a_B$.
Substitute into the joint cap $a_A + a_B = 45$, then plug the solution into either $MAC$ equation for $p_{\text{permit}}$.

options_template.text: $a_A^* = 30$ tons, $a_B^* = 15$ tons, and $p_{\text{permit}} = \$60$/ton
options_template.feedback: Correct. Equating $2a_A = 4a_B$ gives $a_A = 2a_B$. Substituting into $2a_B + a_B = 45$ yields $a_B^* = 15$ tons, $a_A^* = 30$ tons, and $p_{\text{permit}} = 2(30) = 4(15) = \$60$/ton.

options_template.text: $a_A^* = 22.5$ tons, $a_B^* = 22.5$ tons, and $p_{\text{permit}} = \$67.50$/ton
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Uniform Mandate Split): Splitting the $45$-ton cap equally ignores the fact that Factory A can abate at half the marginal cost slope of Factory B.

options_template.text: $a_A^* = 15$ tons, $a_B^* = 30$ tons, and $p_{\text{permit}} = \$60$/ton
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reversed Firm Assignments): Assigning the larger cut to higher-cost Factory B yields $MAC_A = \$30 \ne MAC_B = \$120$, violating equimarginal efficiency.

options_template.text: $a_A^* = 30$ tons, $a_B^* = 15$ tons, and $p_{\text{permit}} = \$120$/ton
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Summed Marginal Costs): Adding $MAC_A + MAC_B = \$60 + \$60 = \$120$ double-counts the permit price; at the optimum each firm's $MAC$ individually equals $p_{\text{permit}} = \$60$.

questions.title: Computing Total Cost Savings: Cap-and-Trade vs. Uniform Mandate
questions.prompt_template: Two plants must jointly cut emissions by $24$ tons. Plant 1 has $MAC_1 = 2a_1$ and Plant 2 has $MAC_2 = 6a_2$ (so each plant's total abatement cost equals the triangle area $\frac{1}{2} \times a_i \times MAC_i(a_i)$). How much total abatement cost does cap-and-trade save compared to a uniform mandate forcing each plant to cut $12$ tons?

hints.text: First calculate total uniform-mandate cost with $a_1 = 12$ and $a_2 = 12$ using triangle areas under each $MAC$ line.
Next solve $2a_1 = 6a_2$ with $a_1 + a_2 = 24$ for the cap-and-trade allocation, compute its total cost, and take the difference.

options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Triangle Factor): Computing $a_i \times MAC_i(a_i)$ without the $\frac{1}{2}$ factor doubles every abatement cost and doubles the true savings ($\$144$).
Diagnostic fallacy (Total Cost Reported as Savings): $\$432$ is the total abatement cost under cap-and-trade ($\$324 + \$108$), not the *savings* relative to the $\$576$ uniform mandate.
Diagnostic fallacy (Halved Savings Error): Dividing the true $\$144$ cost savings by $2$ understates the efficiency gain from permit trading.

questions.topic: Coase Bargaining Range & Net Social Gain
questions.title: Calculating the Coasean Bargaining Range
questions.prompt_template: A workshop's late-night machinery imposes $\$6,500$ in noise damages on an adjacent apartment owner. The workshop can eliminate the noise completely by installing a sound filter costing $\$4,000$, or by shutting down at a profit loss of $\$12,000$. Assuming zero transaction costs and that the workshop holds the legal right to operate without a filter, what lump-sum payment range from the apartment owner to the workshop makes both parties strictly better off, and what is the net social gain?

hints.text: Identify the lowest-cost way to eliminate the noise (filter vs. shutdown).
The workshop requires at least its abatement cost; the apartment owner will pay at most the damages avoided.

options_template.text: Payment between $\$6,500$ and $\$12,000$; net social gain $= \$5,500$
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (High-Cost Option Error): Shutting down ($\$12,000$) is inefficient because damages are only $\$6,500$; the cheaper $\$4,000$ filter makes abatement socially worthwhile.

options_template.text: Payment between $\$4,000$ and $\$6,500$; net social gain $= \$2,500$
options_template.feedback: Correct. The workshop accepts any payment above its $\$4,000$ filter cost, while the apartment owner pays any amount below the $\$6,500$ damage avoided, generating a net social gain of $\$6,500 - \$4,000 = \$2,500$.

options_template.text: Payment between $\$2,500$ and $\$4,000$; net social gain $= \$2,500$
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Below-Cost Offer Error): Any payment below $\$4,000$ fails to cover the workshop's filter expense, so the workshop would refuse the deal.

options_template.text: Payment between $\$4,000$ and $\$6,500$; net social gain $= \$6,500$
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Gross vs. Net Benefit Error): $\$6,500$ is the *gross* damage avoided; subtracting the $\$4,000$ resource cost of the filter gives the *net* social gain of $\$2,500$.

questions.title: Solving for the Optimal Quantity of a Non-Rival Public Good
questions.prompt_template: Two coastal towns share a non-rival flood-alert sensor network. Town A's marginal benefit is $MB_A = 60 - Q$, and Town B's marginal benefit is $MB_B = 40 - Q$ (with $MB_i \ge 0$). If the constant marginal cost of each sensor is $MC = \$36$, what is the socially optimal number of sensors $Q^*$?

hints.text: Sum the two marginal benefit equations vertically ($MSB = MB_A + MB_B$) on the interval where both are non-negative ($0 \le Q \le 40$).
Set $MSB(Q^*) = MC = 36$ and verify that $Q^* \le 40$ so both towns have $MB_i \ge 0$.

options_template.text: $Q^* = 24$ sensors
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Unilateral Provision Error): Solving $MB_A = 36$ ($60 - Q = 36$) gives $24$ sensors—what Town A would buy alone while ignoring Town B's marginal benefit.

options_template.text: $Q^* = 28$ sensors
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Horizontal Summation Fallacy): Summing individual quantities horizontally at $P = \$36$ gives $Q_A(36) + Q_B(36) = 24 + 4 = 28$; non-rival public goods require *vertical* summation.

options_template.text: $Q^* = 32$ sensors
options_template.feedback: Correct. Vertically summing gives $MSB = (60 - Q) + (40 - Q) = 100 - 2Q$ for $0 \le Q \le 40$. Setting $100 - 2Q^* = 36$ yields $2Q^* = 64 \implies Q^* = 32$ sensors (check: $MB_A(32) = \$28$, $MB_B(32) = \$8$, sum $= \$36$).

options_template.text: $Q^* = 64$ sensors
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Slope Summation): Adding intercepts ($60 + 40 = 100$) while forgetting to add the slopes ($-Q - Q = -2Q$) erroneously solves $100 - Q = 36 \implies Q = 64$.

questions.topic: Public Good Provision Beyond the MSB Kink
questions.title: Checking Non-Negative Willingness to Pay Past the Kink
questions.prompt_template: Two neighborhoods share non-rival park benches. Neighborhood 1 has $MB_1 = 70 - Q$, and Neighborhood 2 has $MB_2 = 20 - Q$ (with $MB_i \ge 0$). If constant marginal cost is $MC = \$30$ per bench, what is the socially optimal number of benches $Q^*$?

hints.text: Check the height of $MSB = 90 - 2Q$ right at the kink $Q = 20$ where $MB_2$ hits $\$0$.
Since $MSB(20) = \$50 > \$30$, the optimum lies on the lower segment ($Q > 20$) where $MB_2 = 0$ and $MSB = MB_1$.

options_template.text: $Q^* = 30$ benches
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Negative Willingness-to-Pay Error): Blindly solving $90 - 2Q = 30$ yields $Q = 30$, where $MB_2(30) = -\$10$; willingness to pay cannot be negative.

options_template.text: $Q^* = 20$ benches
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Kink-Stopping Error): At the kink $Q = 20$, Neighborhood 1 still values the next bench at $\$50 > \$30$, so stopping at $20$ forfeits net social surplus.

options_template.text: $Q^* = 60$ benches
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Slope Summation): Solving $90 - Q = 30$ adds intercepts without summing slopes and violates $MB_2 \ge 0$.

options_template.text: $Q^* = 40$ benches
options_template.feedback: Correct. At the kink $Q = 20$, $MSB(20) = \$50 > MC = \$30$, so $Q^* > 20$. On that segment $MB_2 = 0$ and $MSB = MB_1 = 70 - Q$; setting $70 - Q^* = 30$ yields $Q^* = 40$ benches.

questions.title: Calculating Net Social Surplus Gained from Collective Provision
questions.prompt_template: Two districts share a non-rival air-quality monitoring network. District 1 has $MB_1 = 60 - Q$, District 2 has $MB_2 = 36 - Q$ (with $MB_i \ge 0$), and constant marginal cost is $MC = \$40$ per monitor. Acting alone, District 1 buys $Q_1 = 20$ monitors and District 2 free rides ($Q_2 = 0$). How much additional net social surplus is gained by coordinating to reach the socially optimal quantity $Q^*$?

hints.text: Compute $Q^*$ from $MSB = 96 - 2Q = 40$ (valid for $Q \le 36$), and evaluate $MSB$ at the unilateral quantity $Q_1 = 20$.
Calculate the area of the surplus-gain triangle: $\frac{1}{2} \times (Q^* - Q_1) \times (MSB(Q_1) - MC)$.

options_template.feedback: Correct. Setting $96 - 2Q^* = 40$ gives $Q^* = 28$ monitors. At $Q_1 = 20$, $MSB(20) = 96 - 40 = \$56$, so the net surplus gain is $\frac{1}{2} \times (28 - 20) \times (\$56 - \$40) = \frac{1}{2} \times 8 \times \$16 = \$64$.
Diagnostic fallacy (Omitted Triangle Factor): Multiplying $(28 - 20) \times (\$56 - \$40) = \$128$ computes a rectangle instead of the surplus-gain triangle.
Diagnostic fallacy (Total Cost vs. Net Surplus): Multiplying $8$ extra monitors by $MC = \$40$ equals the total *cost* of expansion ($\$320$), not the net welfare gain above cost.
Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong Triangle Height): Using $MC = \$40$ instead of the net marginal benefit gap $MSB(20) - MC = \$16$ yields $\frac{1}{2} \times 8 \times \$40 = \$160$.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Evaluating Peak-Hour Dynamic Bridge Tolls
questions.prompt_template: A metropolitan transit agency proposes replacing a flat all-day bridge toll with dynamic congestion pricing that charges higher tolls during weekday rush hours and very low tolls at midnight. How does economic theory evaluate this design?

hints.text: Think about how the Marginal External Cost ($MEC$) of an additional car varies between rush hour and midnight.
Match the Pigouvian principle $t^* = MEC(Q^*)$ to time-varying traffic congestion.

options_template.text: It is inefficient because a flat toll keeps marginal private cost identical at all hours of the day.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Constant-Externality Assumption): Congestion $MEC$ is near zero on an empty midnight bridge and very high during rush hour, so a flat toll misprices both periods.

options_template.text: It is inefficient because any toll on a public bridge creates deadweight loss by discouraging travel.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Distortion-Free Market Fallacy): During rush hour, an unpriced bridge suffers from over-congestion ($MSC > MB$); a corrective toll *reduces* deadweight loss.

options_template.text: It moves closer to Pigouvian efficiency because each driver's marginal external delay ($MEC$) is large during peak hours and near zero off-peak.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Dynamic tolls align the price of road space with time-varying $MEC$, inducing drivers with flexible schedules to shift off-peak while preserving capacity for high-value rush-hour trips.

options_template.text: It is unnecessary because commuters already pay for their own gasoline and travel time.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Private vs. Social Cost Omission): Drivers internalize their *own* fuel and time ($MPC$), but ignore the cumulative delay and idling emissions they impose on thousands of trailing drivers ($MEC$).

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Empirical Carbon Emissions Data vs. Social Cost of Carbon
questions.title: Interpreting FRED Carbon Emissions Series in Policy Design
questions.prompt_template: An economist retrieves the St. Louis Fed FRED series `EMISSCO2TOTVTTTOUSA` (annual U.S. energy-related carbon dioxide emissions compiled by the U.S. EIA, measured in million metric tons of $\text{CO}_2$). Why is this series alone insufficient to calculate the optimal Pigouvian carbon tax rate $t^*$?

hints.text: Check the units of `EMISSCO2TOTVTTTOUSA` versus the units required for $t^* = MEC(Q^*)$.
Distinguish physical emissions quantities from the dollar marginal external damage per ton.

options_template.text: Because carbon dioxide emissions are a positive externality that requires a subsidy rather than a tax.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Externality Sign Error): Greenhouse gas emissions impose unpriced climate damages ($MEC > 0$), making them a negative externality.

options_template.text: Because `EMISSCO2TOTVTTTOUSA` measures physical emissions volume (million metric tons), whereas setting $t^* = MEC(Q^*)$ also requires estimating the dollar marginal external damage per ton (the social cost of carbon).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Physical emissions data track quantity ($Q$), not marginal monetary harm per ton ($MEC$); calculating $t^*$ requires pairing physical data with estimates of the social cost of carbon.

options_template.text: Because physical $\text{CO}_2$ emissions data can only be used for Coase bargaining, never for Pigouvian taxation.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Instrument Mismatch): Global climate emissions involve billions of dispersed parties with prohibitive transaction costs, making Coase bargaining infeasible and Pigouvian pricing/cap-and-trade the primary tools.

options_template.text: Because Pigouvian taxes depend solely on firms' private marginal costs ($MPC$) and ignore external damages.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Wrong Tax Formula): By definition, a Pigouvian tax equals Marginal External Cost at the optimum ($t^* = MEC(Q^*)$), not $MPC$.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Welfare Effects of Corrective vs. Distortionary Taxes
questions.title: Pigouvian Taxes vs. Taxes in Distortion-Free Markets
questions.prompt_template: A student argues: 'In Chapter 4 we proved that every per-unit excise tax creates deadweight loss, so taxing industrial sulfur emissions must reduce total social welfare.' What is the flaw in this argument?

hints.text: Compare the pre-tax market outcome in a distortion-free market ($MB = MC = MSC$) with a negative-externality market ($MB = MPC < MSC$).
Ask what happens to units eliminated by the tax when $MSC > MB$.

options_template.text: Chapter 4 assumed no externalities ($MPC = MSC$); when $MSC > MPC$, a Pigouvian tax up to $MEC(Q^*)$ eliminates overproduced units where $MSC > MB$, thereby *increasing* net social welfare.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Taxing an undistorted market destroys trades with $MB > MC$, creating DWL; taxing a negative externality stops trades with $MSC > MB$, *eliminating* DWL while raising revenue.

options_template.text: Excise taxes never create deadweight loss in competitive markets when the government spends the tax revenue.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Revenue-Eliminates-DWL Fallacy): In an undistorted market, tax revenue is a transfer and does not recover the surplus lost on foregone mutually beneficial trades.

options_template.text: Sulfur taxes avoid deadweight loss only because producers cannot pass any part of a Pigouvian tax onto buyers.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Incidence Confusion): Buyers and sellers typically share a Pigouvian tax ($P^*$ rises and $P_s$ falls); the welfare gain comes from curbing units where $MSC > MB$, not from tax incidence.

options_template.text: The student is right: Pigouvian taxes always reduce total social welfare, but governments use them solely to raise budget revenue.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Corrective Benefit Omission): A properly set Pigouvian tax unambiguously *increases* total social surplus by removing the negative-externality DWL triangle.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Evaluating California's Cap-and-Trade Cost Advantage
questions.prompt_template: Why does a cap-and-trade system like California's greenhouse gas program achieve a statewide emissions target at lower total cost than a command-and-control mandate requiring every power plant and refinery to cut emissions by the same percentage?

hints.text: Consider how marginal abatement costs ($MAC$) vary across older refineries, newer gas plants, and industrial facilities.
Trace who abates more and who buys allowances when permits can be traded.

options_template.text: Because cap-and-trade lets firms ignore the statewide emissions cap whenever abatement is expensive.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Cap Misunderstanding): Total permits issued are strictly capped at the statewide target; trading redistributes *who* abates without relaxing total emissions.

options_template.text: Because command-and-control mandates always force total emissions to zero, whereas cap-and-trade allows positive emissions.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Target Confusion): Both policies can be set to the exact same total emissions reduction (e.g., $30$ tons); the cost difference arises from *how* abatement is allocated across firms.

options_template.text: Because trading permits eliminates all marginal abatement costs for high-cost facilities without requiring anyone else to abate.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Free-Lunch Fallacy): High-cost firms pay for permits, and the sellers of those permits must perform extra abatement so total emissions still fall by the full cap.

options_template.text: Because permit trading channels greater abatement to facilities with lower marginal abatement costs ($MAC$) and allows high-$MAC$ facilities to buy permits instead, equalizing $MAC$ across the economy.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Allowing permits to trade exploits differences in $MAC$ across heterogeneous plants, meeting the exact same emissions cap at minimum total resource cost.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Property Rights Assignment: Efficiency vs. Income Distribution
questions.prompt_template: A small paper mill discharges effluent into a private pond owned by a single commercial trout farm, and both owners can negotiate with virtually zero transaction costs. If a court shifts the legal property right from the mill (right to discharge) to the trout farm (right to clean water), what does the Coase Theorem predict?

hints.text: Separate two distinct outcomes: (1) the physical level of pollution $Q^*$, and (2) which party pays the other.
Under low transaction costs, does changing who holds the legal right alter $Q^*$ or only wealth distribution?

options_template.text: Pollution drops to zero immediately, and total social surplus falls because the mill must shut down.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (No-Bargaining Assumption): Even if the trout farm holds the right to clean water, the mill can pay the farm for permission to emit up to $Q^*$ whenever the mill's profit gain exceeds the farm's marginal damage.

options_template.text: The socially efficient pollution level $Q^*$ remains unchanged, but income distribution shifts in favor of the trout farm (which now receives compensation instead of paying the mill).
options_template.feedback: Correct. Under clearly defined rights and low transaction costs, Coase bargaining reaches the same efficient $Q^*$ regardless of initial assignment, while ownership determines who pays whom.

options_template.text: Both the efficient pollution level $Q^*$ and the income distribution between the two owners remain completely identical.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Distribution-Invariance Fallacy): Initial property rights strongly affect *income distribution* (who compensates whom), even though the efficient output $Q^*$ is invariant.

options_template.text: Private bargaining breaks down because courts cannot enforce private agreements once property rights change.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Misreading Legal Clarity): A clear court ruling *establishes* the well-defined property right needed for Coase bargaining to proceed smoothly.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Why Coase Bargaining Fails for Regional Smog and Climate Emissions
questions.prompt_template: Why can private Coase bargaining readily resolve a noise dispute between two neighboring businesses, yet fail to solve metropolitan smog or global greenhouse gas emissions?

hints.text: Check the two foundational prerequisites of the Coase Theorem against a problem involving millions of emitters and residents.
Consider negotiation costs, identifying every affected party, and holdout or free-rider incentives.

options_template.text: Because regional smog and carbon emissions have zero marginal external cost ($MEC = 0$).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Damage Error): Both urban smog and climate emissions impose substantial, well-documented external costs.

options_template.text: Because the Coase Theorem applies only to positive externalities, never to negative externalities.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Scope Misconception): The Coase Theorem applies to both negative and positive externalities whenever property rights are clear and transaction costs are low.

options_template.text: Because coordinating millions of dispersed emitters and residents creates prohibitive transaction costs, undefined ambient air rights, and severe holdout/free-rider barriers.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When huge numbers of dispersed people are affected, organizing, negotiating, and enforcing private bargains becomes prohibitively costly, motivating public corrective tools like Pigouvian taxes or cap-and-trade.

options_template.text: Because private businesses are legally prohibited from paying compensation to local residents.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Legal-Ban Fallacy): The barrier is economic (transaction costs and collective-action problems), not a blanket legal ban on private settlements.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: When Does Cap-and-Trade Deliver the Largest Efficiency Advantage?
questions.prompt_template: Compare two industries facing an identical mandatory emissions cut: Industry X consists of firms with nearly identical marginal abatement cost ($MAC$) curves, while Industry Y consists of firms with wildly different $MAC$ curves. Where does switching from a uniform mandate to cap-and-trade yield the larger total cost savings?

hints.text: Ask how much permit trading occurs when every firm already has the exact same $MAC$ at the uniform cut.
Connect gains from permit trade to the spread between firms' marginal abatement costs.

options_template.text: Industry Y, because wider differences in $MAC$ across firms create larger gains from shifting abatement toward low-cost firms via permit trading.
options_template.feedback: Correct. When $MAC$ curves are identical (Industry X), a uniform cut already satisfies $MAC_1 = MAC_2$ and leaves no gains from trade; greater heterogeneity (Industry Y) unlocks larger cost savings.

options_template.text: Industry X, because identical firms find it easiest to agree on a single market permit price.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Homogeneity Misconception): If all firms have identical $MAC$ curves, a uniform mandate already achieves the equimarginal optimum, so permit trading generates zero cost savings.

options_template.text: Both industries experience identical percentage cost savings regardless of $MAC$ differences.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Sensitivity Fallacy): Cost savings under cap-and-trade stem directly from reallocating abatement from high-$MAC$ to low-$MAC$ firms.

options_template.text: Neither industry saves costs under cap-and-trade because paying for permits raises total compliance expenditure.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Transfer vs. Resource Cost Confusion): Permit payments between firms are transfers; society's true resource cost is the sum of physical abatement costs, which falls strictly in Industry Y.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Positive Externality Policy: Basic Research & Vaccines
questions.title: Public Funding for Basic Scientific Research
questions.prompt_template: Private biotech firms invest heavily in patentable late-stage drugs, yet routinely underinvest in foundational basic scientific research whose open discoveries benefit competitors and society broadly. Which economic principle explains this gap and its standard policy remedy?

hints.text: Evaluate whether basic scientific discoveries generate unpriced spillovers ($MEB > 0$) and non-excludable benefits.
Match underinvestment driven by $MSB > MPB$ to the appropriate corrective instrument.

options_template.text: Basic research creates a negative externality ($MSC > MPC$), so governments should levy a Pigouvian tax on university laboratories.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Externality Sign Reversal): Open scientific discoveries generate positive spillover benefits ($MEB > 0$), so taxing them would worsen underprovision.

options_template.text: Basic research generates large positive externalities ($MSB > MPB$) and public-good spillovers that private firms cannot fully capture, justifying public research grants or Pigouvian R&D subsidies.
