options_template.feedback: Correct. Because private firms weigh only their capturable private return ($MPB$) and ignore industry-wide spillovers ($MEB$), public grants and subsidies move investment closer to $Q^*$.

options_template.text: Basic research is a rival common resource, so governments should cap the number of scientific papers published each year.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Common Resource Misclassification): Scientific knowledge is *non-rival* (one researcher using a theorem does not deplete it for others), so capping output would destroy social value.

options_template.text: Private firms underinvest solely because basic research has zero marginal private benefit ($MPB = 0$) and zero marginal social benefit ($MSB = 0$).
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Benefit Fallacy): Basic research often yields massive $MSB$; the market failure arises because the discovering firm captures only a fraction of $MSB$ as private profit.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: How Individual Transferable Quotas Solve Overfishing
questions.prompt_template: How do Individual Transferable Quotas (ITQs)—also called catch shares—address the Tragedy of the Commons in Pacific salmon and other coastal fisheries?

hints.text: Recall why open-access fleets race to harvest fish today even at the expense of future breeding stocks.
Ask how capping total catch and granting enforceable, tradable shares transforms a fisher's private incentive.

options_template.text: They make ocean fish non-rival in consumption so every fleet can harvest unlimited quantities simultaneously.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Physical-Trait Fallacy): No policy can make a harvested fish non-rival; ITQs work by restricting open access (creating enforceable property rights), not by changing fish biology.

options_template.text: They subsidize larger fishing trawlers so vessels can catch fish faster before the season closes.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Race-to-Fish Aggravation): Subsidizing vessel capacity intensifies the race to fish and accelerates stock collapse.

options_template.text: They ban all commercial fishing permanently so the socially optimal harvest equals zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-Harvest Fallacy): Catch shares maintain a positive, biologically sustainable seasonal harvest rather than banning fishing altogether.

options_template.text: They cap total sustainable seasonal catch and grant enforceable, tradable shares, eliminating the race to fish and giving quota holders a direct financial stake in protecting future spawning stocks.
options_template.feedback: Correct. By converting open-access fishing into enforceable, tradable shares of a sustainable cap, ITQs align fishers' long-term asset values with healthy breeding populations.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Ostrom's Institutional Solutions to the Tragedy of the Commons
questions.prompt_template: Before Nobel laureate Elinor Ostrom's empirical research, many analysts assumed common resources could be saved only through centralized government control or full private ownership. What key finding did Ostrom document across real-world local fisheries, irrigation networks, and pastures?

hints.text: Recall the third institutional pathway highlighted in Section 10.3's Bring It Home case study.
Look for the three community-level governance features Ostrom identified.

options_template.text: Local communities automatically preserve common resources without any rules, monitoring, or enforcement.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Rule-Free Optimism): Ostrom explicitly showed that successful self-governance relies on structured institutions—boundaries, monitoring, and sanctions—not uncoordinated goodwill.

options_template.text: Common resources never suffer from overexploitation unless multinational corporations enter the market.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Scale-Only Misconception): Unregulated open-access incentives can deplete local commons among small users just as easily as large ones when governance rules are absent.

options_template.text: Local communities frequently avoid the Tragedy of the Commons without centralized privatization by establishing clear community boundaries, mutual monitoring, and graduated sanctions for rule-breakers.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Ostrom demonstrated that self-governing user communities can sustain common-pool resources effectively through clear membership boundaries, local monitoring, and escalating penalties.

options_template.text: The only sustainable solution is levying a uniform federal Pigouvian tax identical across every local watershed.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Top-Down Exclusivity): Ostrom's core contribution was showing that locally tailored community governance can succeed where uniform top-down mandates fail.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Policy Trade-Off When Technology Adds Excludability
questions.prompt_template: Suppose a city installs automated electronic license-plate readers on an uncongested express bridge, converting it from a free road into a tolled club good. What new economic trade-off arises once a non-rival good becomes excludable?

hints.text: Check the two traits of a club good: excludable (can charge a price) and non-rival (marginal cost of an extra user is near zero).
What happens to social efficiency if the operator sets a high toll ($P > MC \approx 0$) on an *uncongested* bridge?

options_template.text: Exclusion helps finance high fixed construction costs, but charging a positive price above near-zero uncongested marginal cost excludes some users whose marginal benefit exceeds social cost, creating natural-monopoly pricing challenges.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Adding excludability solves free-riding and funds fixed costs, yet any toll above $MC \approx 0$ on an uncongested bridge turns away drivers with $MB > 0$, illustrating the classic club-good/natural-monopoly trade-off.

options_template.text: Exclusion immediately makes the bridge rival in consumption, causing the Tragedy of the Commons.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Excludability vs. Rivalry Mix-Up): Electronic tolling changes *excludability*, not physical rivalry; an uncongested bridge remains non-rival.

options_template.text: Exclusion guarantees perfectly competitive efficiency with zero deadweight loss at any toll the operator chooses.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Unconditional Efficiency Error): Because uncongested $MC \approx 0$, a monopoly toll set strictly above zero creates underutilization deadweight loss.

options_template.text: Exclusion worsens the free-rider problem by allowing more non-payers to cross the bridge.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Effect Reversal): Automated tolling *reduces* free riding by enforcing payment from users.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.title: Matching Distinct Market Failures to Targeted Public Policies
questions.prompt_template: A coastal city faces three simultaneous challenges: (1) funding a non-excludable tsunami siren network, (2) curbing rush-hour traffic jams on its free bay bridge, and (3) boosting low community flu-vaccination rates. Which policy portfolio correctly matches each market failure to its textbook economic remedy?

hints.text: Classify each challenge first: pure public good, common resource/negative externality, and positive externality.
Pair pure public good -> collective tax funding; congestion -> peak-hour Pigouvian toll; positive externality -> Pigouvian subsidy.

options_template.text: (1) Rely on voluntary user fees for sirens, (2) subsidize rush-hour bridge drivers, and (3) tax flu vaccines.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Inverted Incentives): Voluntary fees fail for public goods (free riders), subsidies worsen rush-hour congestion, and taxing vaccines worsens underconsumption.

options_template.text: (1) Issue tradable siren permits, (2) fund free rush-hour bridge crossings via general taxes, and (3) impose a price ceiling on vaccines.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Mismatched Instruments): Permits cap negative externalities rather than funding public goods, free rush-hour crossings worsen congestion, and price ceilings can create shortages.

options_template.text: (1) Use Coase bargaining among all coastal residents, (2) cap total annual bridge crossings at zero, and (3) privatize herd immunity.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Infeasible Extremes): Coase bargaining fails across thousands of residents due to transaction costs, zero bridge crossings ignores $MB > MSC$, and herd immunity is non-excludable.

options_template.text: (1) Finance tsunami sirens collectively through taxation, (2) apply peak-hour congestion tolls on the bridge, and (3) offer a Pigouvian subsidy for flu vaccinations.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Collective tax funding overcomes public-good free riding (1), peak-hour Pigouvian tolls internalize congestion $MEC$ (2), and Pigouvian subsidies internalize vaccination $MEB$ (3).
